title: AWS Lambda and Serverless Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision of the Lambda execution model, triggers, cold starts, timeouts and memory, API Gateway, SQS, SNS and EventBridge, and when serverless is the wrong choice.

chapters.title: Lambda Execution Model
points: Lambda runs a function per event inside a managed execution environment; you pay per request and per GB-second, with no servers to manage
Handler is the entry point: handler(event, context); event is the trigger's JSON payload, context carries request ID, remaining time and memory
Lifecycle phases: Init (download code, start runtime, run code outside the handler), Invoke (run handler), Shutdown; a warm environment is reused so Init is skipped
Invocation types: synchronous (caller waits, e.g. API Gateway), asynchronous (queued, Lambda retries twice, e.g. S3 or SNS), and event source mapping polling (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams)
Interview Point: What happens between an event arriving and your handler running? Why does code outside the handler run only once per environment? Sync vs async invocation: who retries on failure?

chapters.title: Cold Starts, Timeouts and Memory
points: Cold start = new environment needing Init; warm start reuses one; cold starts hit the first request after idle, scale-out bursts and new deployments

Reduce cold starts: smaller packages, lighter runtimes (Node, Python, Go over JVM), init SDK clients outside the handler, SnapStart for Java, Python and .NET, provisioned concurrency to keep environments warm
Memory is 128 MB to 10,240 MB and CPU scales proportionally with it, so more memory can cut duration and cost; tune with Lambda Power Tuning

Timeout defaults to 3 s and maxes at 15 minutes; API Gateway REST APIs default to a 29 s integration timeout (Regional/private REST APIs can raise it by quota request; HTTP APIs max 30 s), so a 15 min function behind a default API fails at 29 s
Interview Point: Why can raising memory make a function cheaper? How do you fix cold starts for a latency-sensitive API? What limits the timeout of an API-fronted Lambda?

chapters.title: Triggers and API Gateway
points: Common triggers: API Gateway, S3 events, SQS, SNS, EventBridge rules and schedules, DynamoDB Streams, Kinesis; each decides sync, async or polling invocation
API Gateway types: HTTP API (cheaper, lower latency, JWT auth, simpler) vs REST API (API keys, usage plans, request validation, WAF, caching) vs WebSocket API
Lambda proxy integration passes the whole request as event and expects a response of {statusCode, headers, body} with body as a string
API Gateway handles auth (IAM, Cognito or Lambda authorizer), throttling, CORS and stage deploys; CORS headers must also be returned by the function in proxy mode
Interview Point: HTTP API or REST API, and when? What shape must a proxy-integration response have? How does API Gateway authenticate callers before invoking Lambda?

chapters.title: SQS, SNS and EventBridge
points: SQS is a pull queue that buffers work: Lambda polls it, batch size default 10, up to 10,000 for standard queues (10 for FIFO), and failed messages return after the visibility timeout
Set queue visibility timeout to at least 6x the function timeout, and attach a dead-letter queue with maxReceiveCount so poison messages stop looping
SNS is push pub/sub fan-out: one publish goes to many subscribers (Lambda, SQS, HTTP, email); with filter policies each subscriber receives only matching messages
EventBridge routes events on a bus by rule patterns to targets, with schedules (cron/rate), SaaS and AWS service events, and schema-based filtering

Choose: SQS to decouple and absorb spikes, SNS to broadcast, EventBridge to route by content across services; SNS fan-out into SQS queues combines both. Interview Point: SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge, and when to combine them? Why does a visibility timeout under 6x the function timeout risk duplicates? What is a DLQ for?

chapters.title: When Not to Use Serverless and Common Mistakes
points: Poor fit: long-running jobs over 15 minutes, steady high-throughput load (always-on containers or EC2 are cheaper), heavy low-latency needs, and large or GPU workloads
Mistake: Lambda calling itself or two functions triggering each other in a loop; set reserved concurrency and billing alarms to cap runaway cost
Mistake: opening DB connections per invocation exhausts the database; use RDS Proxy or a connection pool initialized outside the handler
Mistake: treating the environment as stateful; /tmp and globals may vanish, so keep state in S3, DynamoDB or similar, and make handlers idempotent because retries and SQS deliver at least once
Interview Point: When would you pick containers over Lambda? How do you stop a recursive Lambda loop? Why must handlers be idempotent?

chapters.title: Serverless Cheat Sheet
points: Limits: timeout 15 min, memory 128 MB to 10,240 MB, API Gateway 29 s, async retries 2, SQS batch up to 10,000 (standard, default 10), 10 (FIFO)
Invocation: sync = caller retries; async = Lambda retries then DLQ or destination; polling = queue or stream controls redelivery
Cold start fixes: SnapStart (Java, Python, .NET), provisioned concurrency, small packages, init outside handler
Pick: HTTP API for simple low-cost APIs, SQS to buffer, SNS to fan out, EventBridge to route and schedule
Interview Point: Walk through an order flow using API Gateway, Lambda, SQS and SNS. Which settings protect it from spikes, duplicates and poison messages?
